To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Caesarean delivery is associated with a reduction in bifidobacterial and Bacteroides abundance.

(i) elective caesareans and antibiotic treatment of the mother and/or newborn are associated with reduced bifidobacteria, increased Clostridia, Enterococcus and staphylocci, (ii) emergency caesareans are associated with increased Veillonella, and (iii) the magnitude of dysbiosis depends on the antibiotic type administered.

the gut microbial composition of breastfed infants is impacted in the first weeks of life by four perinatal medical procedures: caesarean birth, maternal intrapartam antibiotics, postnatal hospitalisation, and postnatal antibiotic treatment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the initial gut colonisation of our offspring is shaped by common medical intervention.
the impact of medical interventions on the gut microbiota of the breastfed infant.
the impact of common medical interventions during pregnancy and infancy, on the infant gut microbiota and health outcomes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the gut microbiota is perturbed by perinatal medical intervention, and the extent of the perturbation depends on the specific intervention.
the gut microbiota of the infant is shaped by medical interventions during birth and postnatally, and that the magnitude of these effects depends on the type of intervention and timing of exposure.
caesarean and antibiotic exposure during infancy are associated with a reduction of bifidobacteria, and a shift towards Clostridium, enterococci, staphylococc, enterobacteria and veillonellae.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the infant gut microbiome is highly susceptible to perturbation during early life and that the impact of medical intervention on gut microbiota can be profound, even when the intervention is short term.

caesarean and antibiotic use during pregnancy or early infancy can lead to a reduction in beneficial bifidobacteria, and an increase in potentially pathogenic bacteria, including Enterobacteriaceae and Enterococcaceae.

caesarean birth, maternal IAP, hospitalisation post birth and antibiotic treatment of the newborn are associated with a dysbiotic infant gut microbiota that is characterised by a reduced abundance of bifidobacteria, Bacteroides and Veillonella, and a higher abundance of Clostridium, Enterobacteriaceae and enterococci.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the impact of perinatal medical procedures on the infant gut microbial community is profound and can be long-lasting.
the infant gut microbiota is highly sensitive to common perinatal medical procedures.
medical interventions during birth and the postnatal period can alter the gut microbial composition of the infant, with long-term health implications.
